results.title: Streamlining MLOps with DVC: A Step-by-Step Guide to Reproducible ML Pipelines
results.content: # Streamlining MLOps with DVC: A Step-by-Step Guide to Reproducible ML Pipelines | by Sushant Gautam | Medium. # Streamlining MLOps with DVC: A Step-by-Step Guide to Reproducible ML Pipelines. **In the rapidly evolving field of Machine Learning Operations (MLOps), managing data, code, and models in a streamlined, reproducible way is more important than ever.** Enter **DVC (Data Version Control)** — a powerful tool that allows you to version control large datasets, track dependencies, and easily organize your ML workflow. In traditional software development, version control is handled by Git, which works well for code but struggles with large data files and machine learning artifacts like model files. DVC is designed to fill this gap, providing Git-like version control for datasets, model files, and pipeline stages. ## DVC in Action: A Step-by-Step Pipeline. With DVC, we track this data just as we would with Git, meaning each version of the dataset is saved, and we can revert back to any previous version.

results.content: # Reproducible and upgradable Conda environments with conda-lock. On the one hand, you want to pin all your dependencies to specific versions, so you get reproducible builds. Ideally you’d be able to both have a consistent, reproducible build, and still be able to quickly change your dependencies. You create an `environment.yml` for your dependencies:. If you have to recreate the environment, it will install the latest version of Pandas: you might get different results, or maybe your code won’t run at all. If you create a new environment with this file, you’ll see that many other packages are installed, dependencies of dependencies, and those are dependencies whose versions you didn’t specify:. Once you that environment with all the dependencies installed, you can create new `environment.yml` that has the exact versions of all dependencies, including dependencies of dependencies. For now, we can just notice that every time you create a new environment with this locked dependency file, you will get the *exact same packages installed*.

results.title: Git LFS and DVC: The Ultimate Guide to Managing Large Artifacts in MLOps | by Pablo jusue | Medium
results.content:
Title: Git LFS and DVC: The Ultimate Guide to Managing Large Artifacts in MLOps | by Pablo jusue | Medium
# Navigate to your repositorycd my-ml-project# Start tracking specific file patternsgit lfs track "*.h5"      # Keras modelsgit lfs track "*.pkl"     # Pickled Python objectsgit lfs track "*.parquet" # Parquet filesgit lfs track "*.csv"     # CSV datasetsgit lfs track "*.zip"     # Compressed archivesgit lfs track "data/**"   # Everything in the data directory# IMPORTANT: Commit the .gitattributes file where tracking config is storedgit add .gitattributesgit commit -m "Configure Git LFS tracking patterns". # Adding a large file works like normal Gitgit add models/my_large_model.h5git commit -m "Add trained model"git push# Pulling works transparently toogit pull# Clone with LFS contentgit clone https://github.com/username/repo.git. While Git LFS extends Git to handle large files, DVC reimagines version control for the entire ML lifecycle. # Clone the repository (gets only code and .dvc files)git clone https://github.com/username/repo.gitcd repo# Pull all DVC-tracked filesdvc pull# Or pull only specific filesdvc pull data/training_data.parquet. # Track the dataset formatgit lfs track "*.parquet"git add .gitattributesgit commit -m "Configure LFS tracking for parquet files"# Add the datasetgit add training_data.parquetgit commit -m "Add training dataset v1"git push# Later, update the dataset# (modify training_data.parquet)git add training_data.parquetgit commit -m "Update dataset with new samples"git push# A team member would get the latest versiongit pull# The latest version is automatically downloaded. # Track all large filesgit lfs track "data/**/*.csv" "data/**/*.parquet" "models/*.pkl"git add .gitattributesgit commit -m "Set up LFS tracking patterns"# To run the pipeline, you'd use scripts or a workflow toolpython scripts/process_data.py  # Generates features.parquetpython scripts/train_model.py   # Generates model.pklpython scripts/evaluate.py      # Generates metrics.json# Commit all outputsgit add data/features.parquet models/model.pkl metrics.jsongit commit -m "Run pipeline with latest data"git push. * Git LFS tracks large files but has no awareness of the pipeline structure. # Define the pipeline stagesdvc stage add -n process \    -d scripts/process_data.py -d data/raw_data.csv \    -o data/features.parquet \    python scripts/process_data.pydvc stage add -n train \    -d scripts/train_model.py -d data/features.parquet \    -o models/model.pkl \    python scripts/train_model.pydvc stage add -n evaluate \    -d scripts/evaluate.py -d models/model.pkl -d data/test.csv \    -o metrics.json \    python scripts/evaluate.py# Run the entire pipelinedvc repro# Commit the pipeline definition and outputsgit add dvc.yaml dvc.lock data/features.parquet.dvc models/model.pkl.dvc metrics.jsongit commit -m "Run pipeline with latest data"git pushdvc push. 1. **Using Both Tools Together**: Git LFS for certain assets (documentation images, small datasets) and DVC for ML-specific artifacts (large datasets, models).

results.title: Building a Reproducible Machine Learning Pipeline with MLflow and DVC | by Jake Hotchkiss | Medium
results.content:
Title: Building a Reproducible Machine Learning Pipeline with MLflow and DVC | by Jake Hotchkiss | Medium
# Building a Reproducible Machine Learning Pipeline with MLflow and DVC. This is especially true in real-world deployments, where multiple stakeholders, data versions, and evolving models must be tracked and maintained. In this article, I’ll walk through how I built a machine learning pipeline using MLflow and DVC as part of a recent project in my Master of Science, Data Analytics — Data Engineering program. Although this project was built for school, it mimics real-world MLOps workflows and highlights engineering principles over model development. Using historical flight data from the U.S. Bureau of Transportation Statistics, I trained a Ridge regression model with polynomial features to forecast how late (or early) flights would depart based on scheduled times and destinations. This project leans heavily on the engineering side — wrangling data, implementing version control, and using MLflow to create a reproducible workflow. * **Python**: Data manipulation, model development. * **MLflow**: Experiment tracking and artifact logging. * **scikit-learn**: Model training and feature engineering. To keep the project reproducible and environment-agnostic, I used a `pipeline_env.yaml` file to define all dependencies, including MLflow, NumPy, pandas, and scikit-learn. name: pipeline_envchannels: - conda-forgedependencies: - python=3.10.16 - pandas=2.2.3 - numpy=2.2.4 - seaborn=0.13.2 - matplotlib=3.10.1 - scikit-learn=1.6.1 - mlflow=2.21.3. * Logs each training run in MLflow. Model Performance plot generated at the final step of the pipeline, comparing predicted vs actual departure delays:. * Track **artifacts**: training logs, performance plots, model files. * Calling `mlflow.end_run()` before starting a new final test run. name: deployment-task-2conda_env: pipeline_env.yamlentry_points:  main:    parameters:      num_alphas: {type: int, default: 20}    command: >      python import_data.py &&      python clean_data.py &&      python poly_regressor_Python_1.0.0.py {num_alphas}. mlflow run --experiment-name "Airport Departure Delays" . I used DVC to version the raw dataset without storing the entire CSV in Git. Running `dvc init` and `dvc add data/raw/T_ONTIME_REPORTING.csv` generated a `.dvc` metafile that tracks changes and integrates smoothly into Git workflows. My variation predicts delay across all destination airports given a single origin (MIA), and integrates MLflow tracking using the Python API. This pipeline taught me more than just how to clean data or tune a model — it showed me how real-world machine-learning workflows are engineered, logged, and versioned from end to end.

This repository provides Repo manifests to setup the Yocto build system for reproducible TEE builds. It is a collection of git repositories known as *layers* each of which provides *recipes* to build software packages as well as configuration information. Tell repo to fetch a manifest from this repository and it will fetch the git repositories specified in the manifest and, by doing so, setup a Yocto Project build environment for you! $ repo init -u https://github.com/flashbots/yocto-manifests.git -b main -m .xml # Replace  with tdx-base.xml, tdx-bob.xml, or tdx-buildernet.xml depending on your needs. 1. adjust the yocto build configuration in env\_files for the target image you want to build. * image-buildernet: builds the image for with rbuilder/reth/lighthouse and outputs the image artifacts to */reproducible-build/artifacts-buildernet* (see tdx-buildernet profile).
